content_html:
The fastest computer use for AI agents.

hush-launch.mp4

Hush lets any agent see and drive the apps on your computer, in the background, while you keep working. Read a window, click, type, read it again: 178 ms. The next fastest tool takes 653 ms.

That's fast enough to win one-minute bullet against a 2200 chess.com bot, to play the third movement of the Moonlight Sonata at full tempo with every note on time, and to run ten agents on ten apps at once on one machine, all without anything coming to the front.

How it compares

Same window, same machine, one round of read, click, type, read (details):

Tool Round Works hidden Works on another Space Tool list (MCP)
Hush 178 ms yes yes 972 tokens1
agent-desktop 653 ms yes no 10,514 tokens
cua-driver 1,134 ms yes mostly 50,397 tokens
Peekaboo 3,506 ms no no 13,847 tokens
open-computer-use 4,297 ms yes yes 2,654 tokens

On Cua Driver Bench v2's background tasks, agents on Hush went 15/15 with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and with Claude Haiku 5.5, the user never disturbed once. Sonnet took a median 17.8 s per task.

What an agent sees

An agent reads a window as a short outline, sends a batch of steps, and gets back only what changed:

observe TextEdit
# TextEdit · window "Notes.rtf" 800x600 · focus t1
e1 window "Notes.rtf"
  e2 toolbar
    b1 button "Bold"
    p1 popup "Font" = "Helvetica"
  t1 textarea = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (412 chars)

act TextEdit ["type t1 \" Done.\"", "key cmd+s"]
# 2/2 steps · 0.09 s · settled in 31 ms
~ t1 textarea: = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (412 chars) → = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (418 chars)
+ e3 sheet "Do you want to save changes?"
+   b2 button "Save"
  • Never waits for nothing. Hush listens to the app's accessibility events and answers the moment they stop. It learns each app's pace, so a fast native app is never made to wait like a web view.
  • Tiny on tokens. Short refs that survive re-renders, then only the diffs. A repeat read of an unchanged window is 12 tokens.
  • Stays in the background. Events go to the target app only. Your front app keeps focus, your pointer stays put, your clipboard is untouched.
  • Any agent harness. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, your own loop: as a CLI, an MCP server or a skill.

Tools

Tool What it does
apps Find running and installed apps
observe The outline of a window, then only what changed; focus opens one part
act Run a batch of steps and return the change
timeline Play key and pointer events on a millisecond schedule (music, games, drags)
script Run AppleScript (in process, compiled once) or JXA
see A screenshot of one window or element, for what the outline can't show
record Film a window with an animated agent cursor
hush test, hush save Run desktop tests written as text; save an agent's run as one (CLI)

Steps: click REF|X,Y, double REF, right REF, set REF VALUE, type [REF] TEXT, key COMBO [xN], menu A > B, pick REF OPTION, select REF, focus REF, scroll REF up|down|left|right [N], show REF, drag REF|X,Y to REF|X,Y, wait gone REF | REF | text "T" | 500ms [within 10s], lane, unlane.

Any REF can also be the element as its outline line shows it: click button "Save", type field[2] "Ada". Hush finds it when the step runs, so an agent can act on a window it never read, and a batch can reach into a sheet that an earlier step opened.

Timeline events, one per line: MS down KEY, MS up KEY, MS tap KEY [HOLD], MS down X,Y, MS move X,Y, MS up X,Y, MS tap X,Y [HOLD]. Hush plays them on a real-time thread, under a millisecond off schedule at the median.

Install

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OgnjenAdzic28/hush/main/install.sh | sh

That's it. The installer puts hush in ~/.local/bin and runs hush setup, which asks macOS for Accessibility and Screen Recording for your terminal and installs the Hush skill for Claude Code and in ~/.agents/skills, the shared folder Codex, Cursor, Amp, Cline and most other agents read (plus a rule that lets Codex run hush outside its sandbox). Then ask your agent to do something in an app.

Needs macOS 15 or later. Run hush setup again any time to check permissions or update the skill.

On Linux the same command installs a static binary for x86_64 or arm64, and hush setup checks the accessibility bus, Xvfb and ffmpeg instead. On Debian or Ubuntu that's sudo apt install xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg; on Fedora, sudo dnf install xorg-x11-server-Xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg-free.

Pick your agents: install the skill with the skills CLI instead, which lets you choose from 70+ agents:

npx skills add OgnjenAdzic28/hush --skill hush

Another harness: hush setup --skills-dir <its skills folder>, or use the MCP server:

claude mcp add hush -- hush mcp
# ~/.codex/config.toml
[mcp_servers.hush]
command = "hush"
args = ["mcp"]

From source: cargo install --git https://github.com/OgnjenAdzic28/hush hush, with Rust 1.100 or later (rustup update).

Try it yourself:

hush apps
hush observe Notes
hush act Notes 'click b2' 'type t1 "Groceries"' 'key enter'
hush see Notes --out notes.jpg

Many agents at once

One Hush host serves every agent on your machine. It starts with the first command and goes away after ten idle minutes. Each agent gets its own session with its own refs and diffs. Agents on different apps run in parallel; two agents on the same app take turns, so their clicks and keys never interleave.

Ten sessions hammering one host: 500 calls in 2.2 s, zero errors, observe in 48 ms and see in 28 ms at the median, on one core and 101 MB.

The lane

Agents don't need your screen. The lane step moves a window onto Hush's lane, a virtual display nobody can see, parked off a corner of your main display where the pointer can't reach. Windows there still render, take clicks and keys, and can be captured. Only that window moves, and it comes back to where it was on unlane, the moment you switch to its app, or when the host exits.

On Linux the lane is a hidden X server that Hush starts for itself. Every app an agent opens runs there from the start, whether your desktop is X11 or Wayland.

Limits

Decide what agents may touch, app by app, in ~/.config/hush/limits:

never 1Password, Keychain Access, Messages   # agents can't see these
read Terminal, Mail                          # agents can read these, not act on them
only Notes, TextEdit, Terminal, Mail         # with an only line, every other app is off limits

Names are app names or bundle ids. While any limits are set, script is off, since a script can reach any app. hush apps marks limited apps, and a refused call tells the agent the user chose it, so it reports back instead of trying something else. Every command and new MCP session reads the file, so an edit applies at once. A file with a mistake stops Hush until it's fixed, so nothing runs without the limits by accident.

Recording demos

record films a window while Hush works in it, lane included, and draws an agent cursor into the video: it glides to each click, leans into its motion, dips with a ripple on clicks and carries a name tag. The cursor lives only in the video, and the pacing is real.

hush record Notes
hush act Notes 'click b2' 'type t1 "Groceries"'
hush record Notes --stop --label Claude --out demo.mp4

Desktop tests

A test is a text file: the app, the steps, and expect lines that check the window. It names elements the way the outline shows them, so it runs in any session, on any machine, with no model.

# notes.hush
app Notes
click button "New Note"
type textarea[1] "Groceries"
expect text "Groceries"
expect button "Delete"

hush test notes.hush           # or a folder: hush test tests/desktop

Each file runs in a fresh session and stops at its first failure, saying what the window shows instead (expected = "Milk", but t2 field "Title" = "Mlk"). A failed test leaves its outline and a picture in hush-results/, and with --record a movie of the run. Hush waits for each step to settle instead of sleeping, so a test is as fast as the app and doesn't flake on timing. On Linux, tests run on Hush's hidden display, which works on a CI runner with no screen.

An agent can write the test by doing the task once. Every step a session runs is kept with its refs turned into what the outline showed, so hush save turns the run into a test that replays with no model and no tokens:

hush act Notes 'click b1' 'type t2 "Groceries"'
hush save Notes notes.hush     # app Notes · click button "New Note" · type textarea[1] "Groceries"
hush test notes.hush

Platforms

macOS 15 or later: everything above.

Linux: Hush reads and drives apps through AT-SPI, the accessibility bus GTK, Qt, Firefox, Chromium and LibreOffice share. Apps an agent opens start on Hush's hidden display, where keys, clicks, drags, timelines, see and record all work and none of it can reach your screen. Apps you already had open take clicks, set, type, select and menus through accessibility, and nothing else, so an agent can never type into your window by mistake. cmd+s means Ctrl+S there.

Every change runs the real binary against GNOME Calculator, Mousepad, GNOME Text Editor, FeatherPad (Qt), LibreOffice Writer, Firefox and Google Chrome: start, read, type, read back, picture. It also runs against a real GNOME Shell Wayland session, with an app open on the desktop that Hush reads and clicks without disturbing. Measured on GitHub's Linux runners: observe reads GNOME Calculator's 98 elements in 24 ms, a click settles in 20 to 35 ms, and timeline events land 0.18 ms late at the median.

Windows is next.

Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md. Security reports: SECURITY.md.

License

MIT. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

Footnotes

  1. All seven tools, measured at 0.3.0. The other tool lists were measured on 15 Nov 2026. ↩

content_html_zh:
The fastest computer use for AI agents.

hush-launch.mp4

Hush lets any agent see and drive the apps on your computer, in the background, while you keep working. Read a window, click, type, read it again: 178 ms. The next fastest tool takes 653 ms.

That's fast enough to win one-minute bullet against a 2200 chess.com bot, to play the third movement of the Moonlight Sonata at full tempo with every note on time, and to run ten agents on ten apps at once on one machine, all without anything coming to the front.

比较如何

Same window, same machine, one round of read, click, type, read (details):

Tool Round Works hidden Works on another Space Tool list (MCP)
Hush 178 ms yes yes 972 tokens1
agent-desktop 653 ms yes no 10,514 tokens
cua-driver 1,134 ms yes 大多 50,397 tokens
Peekaboo 3,506 ms no no 13,847 tokens
open-computer-use 4,297 ms yes yes 2,654 tokens

On Cua Driver Bench v2's background tasks, agents on Hush went 15/15 with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and with Claude Haiku 5.5, the user never disturbed once. Sonnet took a median 17.8 s per task.

What an agent sees

An agent reads a window as a short outline, sends a batch of steps, and gets back only what changed:

observe TextEdit
# TextEdit · window "Notes.rtf" 800x600 · focus t1
e1 window "Notes.rtf"
  e2 toolbar
    b1 button "Bold"
    p1 popup "Font" = "Helvetica"
  t1 textarea = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (412 chars)

act TextEdit ["type t1 \" Done.\"", "key cmd+s"]
# 2/2 steps · 0.09 s · settled in 31 ms
~ t1 textarea: = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (412 chars) → = "Meeting notes, 13 Nov. Ship the…" (418 chars)
+ e3 sheet "Do you want to save changes?"
+   b2 button "Save"
  • Never waits for nothing. Hush listens to the app's accessibility events and answers the moment they stop. It learns each app's pace, so a fast native app is never made to wait like a web view.
  • Tiny on tokens. Short refs that survive re-renders, then only the diffs. A repeat read of an unchanged window is 12 tokens.
  • Stays in the background. Events go to the target app only. Your front app keeps focus, your pointer stays put, your clipboard is untouched.
  • Any agent harness. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, your own loop: as a CLI, an MCP server or a skill.

Tools

Tool 它的作用
apps Find running and installed apps
observe The outline of a window, then only what changed; focus opens one part
act Run a batch of steps and return the change
timeline Play key and pointer events on a millisecond schedule (music, games, drags)
脚本 Run AppleScript (in process, compiled once) or JXA
see A screenshot of one window or element, for what the outline can't show
记录 Film a window with an animated agent cursor
hush test, hush save Run desktop tests written as text; save an agent's run as one (CLI)

Steps: click REF|X,Y, double REF, right REF, set REF VALUE, type [REF] TEXT, key COMBO [xN], menu A > B, pick REF OPTION, select REF, focus REF, scroll REF up|down|left|right [N], show REF, drag REF|X,Y to REF|X,Y, wait gone REF | REF | text "T" | 500ms [within 10s], lane, unlane.

Any REF can also be the element as its outline line shows it: click button "Save", type field[2] "Ada". Hush finds it when the step runs, so an agent can act on a window it never read, and a batch can reach into a sheet that an earlier step opened.

Timeline events, one per line: MS down KEY, MS up KEY, MS tap KEY [HOLD], MS down X,Y, MS move X,Y, MS up X,Y, MS tap X,Y [HOLD]. Hush plays them on a real-time thread, under a millisecond off schedule at the median.

安装

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OgnjenAdzic28/hush/main/install.sh | sh

就是这样。 The installer puts hush in ~/.local/bin and runs hush setup, which asks macOS for Accessibility and Screen Recording for your terminal and installs the Hush skill for Claude Code and in ~/.agents/skills, the shared folder Codex, Cursor, Amp, Cline and most other agents read (plus a rule that lets Codex run hush outside its sandbox). Then ask your agent to do something in an app.

Needs macOS 15 or later. Run hush setup again any time to check permissions or update the skill.

On Linux the same command installs a static binary for x86_64 or arm64, and hush setup checks the accessibility bus, Xvfb and ffmpeg instead. On Debian or Ubuntu that's sudo apt install xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg; on Fedora, sudo dnf install xorg-x11-server-Xvfb at-spi2-core ffmpeg-free.

Pick your agents: install the skill with the skills CLI instead, which lets you choose from 70+ agents:

npx skills add OgnjenAdzic28/hush --skill hush

Another harness: hush setup --skills-dir <its skills folder>, or use the MCP server:

claude mcp add hush -- hush mcp
# ~/.codex/config.toml
[mcp_servers.hush]
command = "hush"
args = ["mcp"]

From source: cargo install --git https://github.com/OgnjenAdzic28/hush hush, with Rust 1.100 or later (rustup update).

Try it yourself:

hush apps
hush observe Notes
hush act Notes 'click b2' 'type t1 "Groceries"' 'key enter'
hush see Notes --out notes.jpg

Many agents at once

One Hush host serves every agent on your machine. It starts with the first command and goes away after ten idle minutes. Each agent gets its own session with its own refs and diffs. Agents on different apps run in parallel; two agents on the same app take turns, so their clicks and keys never interleave.

Ten sessions hammering one host: 500 calls in 2.2 s, zero errors, observe in 48 ms and see in 28 ms at the median, on one core and 101 MB.

The lane

Agents don't need your screen. The lane step moves a window onto Hush's lane, a virtual display nobody can see, parked off a corner of your main display where the pointer can't reach. Windows there still render, take clicks and keys, and can be captured. Only that window moves, and it comes back to where it was on unlane, the moment you switch to its app, or when the host exits.

On Linux the lane is a hidden X server that Hush starts for itself. Every app an agent opens runs there from the start, whether your desktop is X11 or Wayland.

限制

Decide what agents may touch, app by app, in ~/.config/hush/limits:

never 1Password, Keychain Access, Messages   # agents can't see these
read Terminal, Mail                          # agents can read these, not act on them
only Notes, TextEdit, Terminal, Mail         # with an only line, every other app is off limits

Names are app names or bundle ids. While any limits are set, script is off, since a script can reach any app. hush apps marks limited apps, and a refused call tells the agent the user chose it, so it reports back instead of trying something else. Every command and new MCP session reads the file, so an edit applies at once. A file with a mistake stops Hush until it's fixed, so nothing runs without the limits by accident.

Recording demos

record films a window while Hush works in it, lane included, and draws an agent cursor into the video: it glides to each click, leans into its motion, dips with a ripple on clicks and carries a name tag. The cursor lives only in the video, and the pacing is real.

hush record Notes
hush act Notes 'click b2' 'type t1 "Groceries"'
hush record Notes --stop --label Claude --out demo.mp4

Desktop tests

A test is a text file: the app, the steps, and expect lines that check the window. It names elements the way the outline shows them, so it runs in any session, on any machine, with no model.

# notes.hush
app Notes
click button "New Note"
type textarea[1] "Groceries"
expect text "Groceries"
expect button "Delete"

hush test notes.hush           # or a folder: hush test tests/desktop

Each file runs in a fresh session and stops at its first failure, saying what the window shows instead (expected = "Milk", but t2 field "Title" = "Mlk"). A failed test leaves its outline and a picture in hush-results/, and with --record a movie of the run. Hush waits for each step to settle instead of sleeping, so a test is as fast as the app and doesn't flake on timing. On Linux, tests run on Hush's hidden display, which works on a CI runner with no screen.

An agent can write the test by doing the task once. Every step a session runs is kept with its refs turned into what the outline showed, so hush save turns the run into a test that replays with no model and no tokens:

hush act Notes 'click b1' 'type t2 "Groceries"'
hush save Notes notes.hush     # app Notes · click button "New Note" · type textarea[1] "Groceries"
hush test notes.hush

平台

macOS 15 or later: everything above.

Linux: Hush reads and drives apps through AT-SPI, the accessibility bus GTK, Qt, Firefox, Chromium and LibreOffice share. Apps an agent opens start on Hush's hidden display, where keys, clicks, drags, timelines, see and record all work and none of it can reach your screen. Apps you already had open take clicks, set, type, select and menus through accessibility, and nothing else, so an agent can never type into your window by mistake. cmd+s means Ctrl+S there.

Every change runs the real binary against GNOME Calculator, Mousepad, GNOME Text Editor, FeatherPad (Qt), LibreOffice Writer, Firefox and Google Chrome: start, read, type, read back, picture. It also runs against a real GNOME Shell Wayland session, with an app open on the desktop that Hush reads and clicks without disturbing. Measured on GitHub's Linux runners: observe reads GNOME Calculator's 98 elements in 24 ms, a click settles in 20 to 35 ms, and timeline events land 0.18 ms late at the median.

Windows is next.
